newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel mulls higher VAT to offset income tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: Waigel mulls higher VAT to offset income tax cuts.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Wednesday it would be acceptable to raise value added tax (VAT) to finance the government's planned cut in income taxes.

In an interview in the daily Sueddeutsche Zeitung, Waigel repeated that the government wanted to lower the basic income tax rates and cut exemptions to finance the reform, which envisages tax cuts totalling up to 30 billion marks.
"If that is not sufficient, I would consider it legitimate to shift from direct to indirect taxes," Waigel said.
"In many areas, we have the highest direct tax rates. We could achieve a reduction here and compensate it through our relatively low indirect tax rates, such as value added tax."
Waigel's comments came on the heels of a meeting of the government's tax commission, which is expected later this month to present plans for a broad reform of Germany's tax system.
His statements are likely to fuel speculation that the government could surprise voters with a post-election rise in value added tax, which is currently 15 percent.

Opposition politicians and some economists have long expected the government to raise indirect taxes and have suggested that value added tax could rise as much as two points in 1999, after the next general election in 1998.

Waigel also took the opportunity to say that the solidarity tax, a 7.5-percent surcharge on income tax bills to finance German unification, could not be abolished without secure financing. The tax raises around 30 billion marks in revenue each year needed to rebuild the eastern German economy.
The centre-right coalition government agreed to cut the tax to 5.5 percent next year but has been strained over differences in how quickly to phase out the unpopular tax.

While Chancellor Helmut Kohl's junior coalition partners, the Free Democrats, want to scrap the tax in the year 2000, Kohl's Christian Democrats and Waigel's Bavarian Christian Social Union have said this could not be financed.
"No one has been able to show me so far how the federal government would be able to digest the loss of the solidarity tax all at once in the year 2000," Waigel said.
